Survival Analysis of the Mayo Clinic PBC Trial

Kaplan-Meier estimation and Cox proportional hazards regression

Author

Isla Yao

Published

November 18, 2026

1. Introduction

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic autoimmune liver disease in which the small bile ducts are progressively destroyed, eventually leading to cirrhosis and liver failure. This analysis uses data from the Mayo Clinic randomised placebo-controlled trial of D-penicillamine, conducted between 1974 and 1984 and distributed with the R `survival` package. The aims were to (1) compare time to death or liver transplant between the treatment groups using Kaplan-Meier estimation and the log-rank test, and (2) identify prognostic factors using a Cox proportional hazards model including treatment, age, sex, bilirubin and albumin.

2. Setup

Code 
library(survival)

3. Data preparation

Code 
pbc_trial <- subset(pbc, !is.na(trt))

pbc_trial$event <- as.integer(pbc_trial$status >= 1)

pbc_trial$trt <- factor(pbc_trial$trt,
                        levels = c(1, 2),
                        labels = c("D-penicillamine", "Placebo"))

pbc_trial$time_years <- pbc_trial$time / 365.25

We restricted the analysis to the 312 patients who took part in the randomised trial, excluding 106 non-randomised patients with no treatment assignment. The outcome is a composite of death or liver transplant: 144 patients experienced the event (125 deaths and 19 transplants), and 168 were censored. Follow-up time was converted from days to years.

4. Kaplan-Meier survival curves

Code 
km_fit <- survfit(Surv(time_years, event) ~ trt, data = pbc_trial)

Call:

                      N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
trt=D-penicillamine 158       75     72.9    0.0595     0.121
trt=Placebo         154       69     71.1    0.0611     0.121

 Chisq= 0.1  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.7
The Kaplan-Meier curves for the two treatment groups overlap throughout follow-up and cross several times. Median time to death or transplant was 7.1 years (95% CI 6.4–11.2) in the D-penicillamine group and 8.7 years (95% CI 7.7–10.5) in the placebo group, with widely overlapping confidence intervals. The log-rank test showed no evidence of a difference between groups (χ² = 0.1, df = 1, p = 0.7). Estimates beyond about 10 years are less reliable because few patients remained at risk.

5. Cox proportional hazards model

Code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(pbc_trial$bili, main = "Bilirubin", xlab = "mg/dL")
hist(log2(pbc_trial$bili), main = "log2(Bilirubin)", xlab = "log2(mg/dL)")
Code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
Code 
cox_fit <- coxph(Surv(time_years, event) ~ trt + age + sex + log2(bili) + albumin,
                 data = pbc_trial)
summary(cox_fit)

Bilirubin was strongly right-skewed, so it was entered on the log2 scale; hazard ratios for bilirubin therefore refer to a doubling of its value. After adjustment, treatment was not associated with the hazard of death or transplant (HR for placebo vs D-penicillamine 1.07, 95% CI 0.77–1.50, p = 0.69), consistent with the log-rank test. Bilirubin was the strongest predictor: each doubling was associated with a near two-fold increase in hazard (HR 1.95, 95% CI 1.72–2.20). Higher albumin was protective (HR 0.33 per 1 g/dL, 95% CI 0.22–0.50), and older age was associated with higher hazard (HR 1.02 per year, 95% CI 1.00–1.04; roughly 21% per decade). The hazard was lower in women, but this was not statistically significant (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.45–1.12), possibly reflecting the small number of men in the trial. The model showed good discrimination (concordance 0.82).

6. Checking the proportional hazards assumption

Code 
ph_test <- cox.zph(cox_fit)
ph_test
            chisq df    p
trt        0.4161  1 0.52
age        0.6546  1 0.42
sex        0.0379  1 0.85
log2(bili) 0.2532  1 0.61
albumin    1.8617  1 0.17
GLOBAL     3.7331  5 0.59
Code 
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in 1:5) {
  plot(ph_test[i])
  abline(h = coef(cox_fit)[i], col = "red", lty = 2)
}

The proportional hazards assumption was assessed using scaled Schoenfeld residuals. There was no evidence of violation for any covariate (all p > 0.15) or globally (p = 0.59). The smoothed residual plots were broadly flat for all covariates; the albumin curve suggested a slight weakening of its protective effect later in follow-up, but this was not statistically significant (p = 0.17). Wider confidence bands at later times reflect the smaller number of patients still at risk.

7. Discussion

### Main findings D-penicillamine showed no benefit over placebo, either in the unadjusted Kaplan-Meier comparison or after adjustment for other covariates. In contrast, markers of liver function were strong prognostic factors: higher bilirubin and lower albumin were both associated with a substantially higher hazard of death or transplant, and older age was associated with a modest increase in hazard. The model discriminated well (concordance 0.82), and the proportional hazards assumption appeared reasonable. ### Limitations - **Composite endpoint.** Death and transplant were combined into a single event. Transplant is a treatment decision rather than a disease outcome, and it prevents death from liver disease from being observed. A competing-risks approach (e.g. cause-specific hazards or Fine-Gray models) would separate the two outcomes. - **Linearity.** Age, log2(bilirubin) and albumin were assumed to act linearly on the log-hazard; this was not formally checked (e.g. with martingale residuals or splines). - **Small number of men**, which limits the precision of the sex effect. - **Historical data.** The trial predates current treatment (ursodeoxycholic acid), so absolute risks may not apply to patients today. ### Next steps The `pbcseq` dataset contains repeated biomarker measurements for the same patients. A natural extension is a joint model linking the longitudinal trajectory of bilirubin to the hazard of death or transplant.

References
